zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical coverage was cross-checked after independent scan reading against the supplied NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510 (CC BY 4.0). The scan, not the lexical index, determines this transcription’s spelling, typeface, and lineation.

lines.note: The example continues the preceding entry: the pen cannot exhaust the matter in writing. The visible aqiarazu is retained; its internal qia is not silently regularized to an expected Japanese expression.

runs.text: acabar de eſcreuer, ou eſgotar com a pena.

lines.note: Completes the preceding negative construction: one cannot finish writing about it or exhaust it with the pen. Eſgotar is the Portuguese verb for exhausting a subject.
Quanjǒſu and quanjǒji are alternative literary names for a writing brush, explicitly identified by Fude. The two carons and the long ſ in the first form are distinct printed details.

Completes pena de escrever, a writing implement. The upright S. is the written-register label, not part of the Portuguese noun phrase. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

runs.text: Numero de vezes que hum Bonzo

lines.note: Quanju here concerns the number of recitations undertaken by a Buddhist cleric. The definition develops across the next four physical lines.

runs.text: lẽ, ou promete de ler o Foquequiǒ por algum de

lines.note: The cleric reads, or promises to read, the Lotus Sutra for a deceased person. Foquequiǒ is the embedded Japanese title, here in italic type; its final mark is a caron. De continues into funto without a supplied hyphen.

runs.text: funto, offerecendo este papel amarrado em hũ

lines.note: Funto completes defunto. The paper recording the recitations is offered tied to a branch; hũ abbreviates the indefinite article and is not expanded.

runs.text: ramo à peßoa aquem quer moſtrar que faz esta

lines.note: The branch is presented to the person whom the cleric wishes to inform of this pious act. The printed aquem remains joined.
Obra pia completes the account of the commemorative religious undertaking. This short continuation belongs to the preceding Quanju definition.

runs.text: Certo officio, ou cargo de Bonzos que

lines.note: This second Quanju names a Buddhist office rather than the preceding recitation count. The scan supports Certo officio, correcting the fused and misread OCR form.
Completes the office definition by specifying some supervisory authority over other clerics. Algũa retains its printed abbreviation tilde.

runs.text: Paßo onde ſe paga algũa porta-

lines.note: Quanmon is a checkpoint or passage where a toll is paid. The Portuguese portagem is physically divided after porta-.
Gem completes portagem, the toll just mentioned. The abbreviation &c. closes the definition on this short physical row.
Quannen denotes contemplation; Quannen quãbô supplies a compound expression interpreted on the following row as meditation on the religious law. The repeated headword lacks the OCR intrusion i.

The main text translates the preceding compound as meditation on the law. At the far right, the parenthesis and Rey. supply the displaced completion of Criados del on the following physical row; they are not part of the meditation gloss.
Quannin is explained by Teiuǒno xinca, the sovereign's retainers. Its Portuguese Criados del is completed by the displaced Rey. above, not by the next entry.
Quanqe is explained through teaching and exhortation, Voxiye ſuſumuru. The Portuguese explanation continues with doutrinar on the next physical row.
Completes ensinar with instructing and exhorting. The scan shows one continuous word doutrinar, not the OCR split do utrinar.

runs.text: Caſa de nobres como de Cũgues, &c.

lines.note: A separate Quanqe denotes a noble household, with court nobles given as the example. Cũgues is visibly capitalized and occurs within the Portuguese explanation.
Quanqen and its Japanese explanation Quanji miru concern contemplation or seeing reflectively. The artificial OCR space within Quanji is removed; the Portuguese alternative continues below.
Conſiderando ver completes the reflective-seeing explanation of Quanqen. It is a Portuguese paraphrase, not another Japanese form.

This different Quanqen means limited knowledge. The following image of looking at the sky through a narrow tube explains the restriction metaphorically. The final e of que sits low at the right edge but belongs to this word, not a separate body row.

runs.text: vè pouco do ceo por hum canudo delgado post

lines.note: The narrow tube is held to the eye. Canudo corrects OCR carudo; the final o of posto is visibly displaced down and right beyond post, so its exceptional placement is retained instead of dropping the letter.
No olho completes the tube image. Quanqenno vcagaiuo naſu introduces the corresponding Japanese expression for making a narrowly limited observation.

runs.text: Saber muito pouco dalgũa arte, ou ſciencia

lines.note: The example is translated as knowing very little of an art or science. The printed dalgũa and ſciencia are retained rather than modernized.

runs.text: como quem vè pouco do ceo por hum canudo

lines.note: The translation repeats the comparison with seeing only a small part of the sky through a tube. The definition continues into the short adjective below.
Delgado completes the description of the narrow tube. Its indentation identifies a continuation, not a fresh headword.
Quanqua is explained by the Japanese terms for a widowed woman and a widowed man. Voto- continues as co on the following physical row.
Co completes votoco. The Portuguese names a widower and widow; Viuuo has two adjacent u types, not OCR Viuo.
Quanqua codocu begins a list of socially unsupported people. The initial Q is roman, not an italic O, and the enumeration continues below.
The Japanese list continues with a widowed man, an orphan, and a person alone. Viuua begins the Portuguese enumeration that follows.
Continues the Portuguese list with widower, orphan, and an unsupported person. The mark after viuuo is a colon; OCR e did not represent a printed conjunction there.

runs.text: que não tem aquem ſe encoste.

lines.note: Completes the unsupported-person description: there is no one to lean on. Encoste corrects the OCR misreading of t as l; the older joined aquem remains.
Quanquacu is glossed as a tomb or burial place. The short Portuguese definition is complete on this row.
Quanquanto is explicitly classified as an adverb, meaning at ease. Italic Vt, introduces the example of an untroubled way of life.
Yǔyǔquanquanto xite curaſu describes living at leisure or without anxiety. The repeated long-u marks are carons; the Portuguese Leuar boa continues below.
Vida, & deſcanſada completes the translation: leading a good, restful life. The adjective is part of the Portuguese sentence begun above.
Quanracu, explained by rejoicing and enjoying oneself, denotes pleasures or satisfactions. Conten- begins a Portuguese word split across the physical rows.
Tamentos completes contentamentos. Quanracuuo qiuamuru means enjoying pleasures to the fullest; the following Go- is Portuguese gozar, not Japanese go.
Zar completes gozar and the translation speaks of many pleasures. The upright S. marks written usage. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
This Quanracu is identified with Vazzurai, illness, and is unrelated to the preceding pleasure sense. The double z is retained in the Japanese synonym.
Quanrei names a particular rank or office. Nome corrects OCR Nomo; the brief gloss does not itself specify the full institutional history.
Quanri is crown and footwear, explained by Camuri and cutçu. The damaged headword is supported by its repetition in the next row; calçado is divided without adding an unprinted hyphen.
Do completes calçado. Quanri zǒuo vonajǔ xezu says that crown and shoes do not share the same storage place; the Portuguese Coroa begins as Co at the right edge without a supplied hyphen.

runs.text: roa, & çapatos não ſe poem no meſmo gudão. i

lines.note: Roa completes Coroa; crown and shoes are not placed in the same gudão. The final explanatory i leads into the figurative social interpretation below; the source has a stop after gudão and no supplied comma after i.

runs.text: Os altos, & os baixos não tem o meſmo lugar

lines.note: Explains the proverb: people of high and low rank do not occupy the same place. The absence of final punctuation in the baseline is consistent with the visible right edge.

Quanſat concerns considering or conjecturing, supported by Mi ſaſſuru. Enlargement favours the anomalous printed conjeiutar rather than silently restoring conjeiturar. The final ve likewise lacks a secure r of expected ver; both readings remain nonblocking caveats.
Completes the explanation as seeing through consideration. The OCR garble is replaced by the visible Portuguese phrase; this is indented body text above the bottom rule.

runs.text: Caldeirão, ou panella de ferro do

lines.note: Quanſu is an iron kettle or pot used for tea. The scan supports panella and ferro, restoring the omitted letters in both OCR words.
Chanoyu completes the tea-ceremony context of the iron vessel. It is a Japanese term embedded in the preceding Portuguese sentence; the local printed type remains italic.
Quantai describes lax neglect; Rǒjeqi identifies the associated discourtesy or offence. The visible initial is R, not OCR B, and Deſ- starts the Portuguese descortesia.

runs.text: corteſia, ou agrauo que hum faz a alguem por

lines.note: Corteſia completes deſcorteſia. The definition concerns an affront or discourtesy that one person does to another.

runs.text: deſcuido, ou priguiça: posto q̃ ja commummente

lines.note: The original sense is attributed to carelessness or laziness, before a qualification about current usage. Printed priguiça and abbreviated q̃ are retained.

runs.text: ſe toma por crime, ou deſcorteſia feita contra

lines.note: The qualification says that the term is commonly taken to mean a crime or discourtesy committed against someone. This broader usage is not a separate entry.
Alguem completes the person-directed offence definition. The short indented row closes Quantai before Quantat begins.

runs.text: O cair bem, & aßentar com o en-

lines.note: Quantat describes arriving at a sound understanding of a subject. The scan reads aßentar and en-, correcting the OCR additions in aßtentar and oer-.

runs.text: tendimento nas couſas que medita, &c. S.

lines.note: Tendimento completes entendimento: settling one's understanding on the things contemplated. Upright S. marks written usage. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Quantô is identified with Tôgocu, the eastern provinces. Both long-o marks are circumflexes rather than carons.

runs.text: que eſtão pera aparte do Oriente.

lines.note: The regions are situated toward the east. The visible capital O corrects Griente; the printed joined aparte is preserved.
Quanxacu denotes honours and wealth. The example begins Quã-, with a visible abbreviation tilde representing the nasal material before the continuation xacu.
Xacu completes the abbreviated Quã- above. Mini amaru means that honours and wealth exceed what befits oneself; the Portuguese tenho is divided after te-.

runs.text: nho de ſobejo, ou em abundancia.

lines.note: Nho completes tenho, followed by having more than enough or in abundance. The visible ſobejo corrects OCR ſobeſo without replacing the historical expression.

runs.text: Dinheiro que ſe dà por ſubir a algũa

lines.note: This Quanxen means money paid to rise to a dignity. The entire Portuguese gloss is italic; the OCR's isolated roman e and its spurious terminal hyphen are removed.
Dignidade completes the description of money paid for advancement to an office or rank. It is not an independent entry.
This second Quanxen is strung cash, explicitly Tçunaidaru jeni. Enfia- begins the Portuguese participle for coins threaded onto a cord, rather than OCR enfpa-.
Das completes enfiadas; em corda specifies that the cash coins are threaded on a cord. This sense is distinct from payment for office above.
Quanxin is explained as a rejoicing heart, Yorocobu cocoro. Its Portuguese alegre is divided at the physical line ending.

runs.text: gre, & eſperto pera fazer algũa couſa, &c.

lines.note: Gre completes alegre. The heart is also ready or alert to perform something, explaining the willing disposition conveyed by the headword.
Quanxô is a calling bell, explicitly Yobu cane. The artificial space after Q is removed, while the circumflex on ô remains.

runs.text: que ſe chama, & ajunta a gente.

lines.note: The bell calls and gathers people together. This functional explanation completes the instrument definition rather than adding a separate sense.
Quanxocu, explained by Camurito xocu, denotes ranks and offices. The Portuguese list continues below with administrative posts.
Officios and cargos complete the range of offices and official responsibilities. The row is a continuation of the rank-and-office entry.
Quanyet is glossed by the Japanese verb Yorocobi, u and Portuguese Alegrarſe, to rejoice. The final t is the dictionary's checked-coda spelling, not an omitted syllable to restore.

runs.text: Brandura com que alguem ſe ha

lines.note: Quanyǔ denotes leniency or gentleness in one's treatment of someone. The definition continues by explaining how punishment or pressure is moderated.

runs.text: mais piadoſamente, & deixa de apertar, ou ca-

lines.note: The lenient person behaves more mercifully and refrains from pressing or punishing another. The Portuguese caſtigar is divided after ca-.
Completes caſtigar a outro, punishing another person. OCR outrouor contains trailing interference not supported as additional printed text.
Quanzǒ is identified simply as an herb or flower of that name. The reading aßi chamada replaces OCR corruption; the gloss alone does not justify a species identification.
Quaqet, literally explained as Fino ana, is a hole or cavern containing fire. Its final t is retained without expansion.
The definition specifies burning fire; Quaqetni tobicomu illustrates jumping into the fire-pit. The example's initial Q belongs to the same word, not a detached OCR token.

runs.text: tarſe dentro na coua do fogo.

lines.note: Tarſe completes Botarſe, casting oneself into the fiery hole. The complete physical row is an explanation of the example above.
Quaqi is the force or quality of fire, explicitly Fino qi. The damaged Portuguese words read Força, qualidade, and fogo, not the OCR alternatives.
This Quaqiǒ denotes a fire-pit, again explained by Fino ana. The damaged initial sequence is Quaqiǒ, not OCR guauiǒ.
This next Quaqiǒ instead denotes floral fragrance, explained by Fanano niuoi. The identical-looking headword must not be merged with the preceding fire-pit entry.
Ou flor completes the gloss as the scent of a rose or flower. The small terminal stop is visible on reinspection; the indented continuation remains separate from the following haste entry.
Quaqiǔ means great haste. The word has a final long-u caron; the OCR space after the capital Q is spurious.
Quaqiǔna is the adjectival form, describing something very hurried. The scan supports ǔna rather than the OCR's malformed fna.
Quaqiǔ is then identified as an adverb. The short Adu. refers back to the haste sense rather than supplying another substantive definition.
Quaqua is explained by the fruits of grasses or herbs and of trees. The Portuguese develops the same distinction across this and the next row.
Completes the contrast between fruit borne by herbs and by trees. The older spelling fruita and joined daruores are retained.
Quara, also called Caqe natǒ, is introduced as a kind of stole. The first letter of natǒ is n, not OCR m; the following lines describe the Buddhist garment.

runs.text: que trazem os Bonzos deitada do peſcoço como

lines.note: The Buddhist clerics wear the stole from the neck; como begins a comparison with deacons. The visible como replaces the OCR's coua.

runs.text: Diaconos ajuntando as pontas nos peitos com hũ

lines.note: The comparison continues: the ends are brought together at the chest with an ivory ring, specified below. Pontas and hũ replace OCR pontar and he.
The fastening is a ring of ivory. There is no further printed phrase after marfim.; the OCR's extra words came from interference, not another body row.
Quaracu is the royal capital, explained by Fanano Miyaco. Miyaco is roman Japanese; Corte del Rey begins the italic Portuguese definition.

runs.text: ou cidade principal onde reſide o Rey.

lines.note: The royal court is further explained as the principal city where the king resides. Principal onde reſide is legible despite the slant and replaces the OCR corruption.

zones.note: Catchword anticipating Quaran on the following page.
